title: Raghupati Upadhyaya
html:
A Pandita from Tirhut

Raghupati Upadhyaya was a Vaishnava scholar and poet whose meeting with Sri Chaitanya in the house of Vallabha Bhatta entered the “Chaitanya-charitamrita” for ever. Krishnadasa Kaviraja calls him Raghupati Upadhyaya, and more often simply Upadhyaya or Raghupati; for Govinda-deva in the “Gaura-krishnodaya” he is “Upadhyaya Raghupati,” and in Srila Rupa Gosvami's “Padyavali” his verses are signed “Raghupati-upadhyaya.” The biographies call him Sri Raghupati Upadhyaya.

He came from Tirhut (Trihut), also called Mithila — a region in the north of present-day Bihar; according to the biographies, from the subdivision of Sitamarhi in the district of Darbhanga. The “Charitamrita” introduces him in just this way — “a pandita from Tiruhita.” Srila Bhaktivinoda Thakura in the “Amrita-pravaha-bhashya” explains that Tirhut is the land of Mithila, and Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati in the “Anubhashya” that four districts now make up Tirhut: Saran, Champaran, Muzaffarpur and Darbhanga.1 From the same region came Paramananda Puri as well, the Lord's close companion in Nilachala.

By birth Raghupati was a brahmana. The biographies remember him as a famous scholar, a great Vaishnava, a mahabhagavata and a noble man; Kaviraja calls him a pandita, a great Vaishnava and a great soul. Nothing more is known of his life in this world: the sources name neither his parents nor his family, nor the year and day of his appearance, nor when and where he left this world. Nor are his days found in the Vaishnava calendar of the Sri Chaitanya Saraswat Math.

A Disciple of Madhavendra Puri

Raghupati was a disciple of Sri Madhavendra Puri. We learn this from Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati's “Gaudiya-bhashya” on the “Chaitanya-bhagavata” (Adi 9.154): among Madhavendra's disciples he names Ishvara Puri, Advaita, Paramananda Puri, Brahmananda Puri, Ranga Puri, Pundarika Vidyanidhi and Raghupati Upadhyaya. The biographies rely on this commentary too; in their lists Raghupati stands beside Pundarika Vidyanidhi, the Sanodiya brahmana and Keshava Bharati. The “Chaitanya-bhagavata” and the “Charitamrita” themselves do not say this.2

In the House of Vallabha Bhatta

Returning from Vrindavana, Sri Chaitanya stayed at Prayaga. There Sri Rupa and his brother Anupama came to Him, and then the scholar Vallabha Bhatta, who lived in the village of Adail across the Yamuna, opposite Prayaga, invited the Lord to his home and brought Him there by boat.3 Already in the boat the Lord held back the feelings that had seized Him. Srila Bhaktivinoda Thakura explains why: that place was almost devoid of prema, and Vallabha Bhatta was much given to argument (“Amrita-pravaha-bhashya” on CC, Madhya 19.83). Where and before whom to reveal His love, the Lord Himself decides; His restraint is not weakness but His will.

In Adail Vallabha washed the Lord's feet and fed Him, and once the Lord had lain down to rest, he sat and pressed His feet himself. It was then, in the presence of Rupa and Anupama, that Raghupati arrived:

“At that time Raghupati Upadhyaya arrived, a pandita from Tirhut, a great Vaishnava and a noble soul. He came and bowed at the Lord's feet, and the Lord said to him: ‘May your mind rest in Krishna.’ Hearing this, Upadhyaya was delighted at heart. The Lord said to him: ‘Describe Krishna to Me.’” (CC, Madhya 19.92–94)

Govinda-deva in the “Gaura-krishnodaya” tells of these days differently:

“Him, like the hot-rayed [sun], staying there awaiting the arrival of Rupa, Vallabha Bhatta and Upadhyaya Raghupati invited daily to their homes and served.” (“Gaura-krishnodaya” 14.63)4

Two Verses

The Lord wished to hear about Krishna, and Raghupati gladly did as He asked:

“He recited a verse of his own about Krishna's pastimes, and hearing it, Mahaprabhu was overwhelmed with great love.

‘Let those who fear worldly existence worship — some the shruti, others the smriti, still others the Mahabharata. But here I bow to Nanda, in whose courtyard the Supreme Brahman plays’ (Padyavali, 126).” (CC, Madhya 19.95–96)

Srila Bhaktisiddhanta in the “Anubhashya” shows whom the poet leaves behind: the “some” who worship the shruti are not servants of Hari but seekers of liberation; the “others” who hold to the smriti are karmis, hungry for the fruits of their rites; and the “Mahabharata” is gladly read by all the people of this world. What drives them all is fear of the round of birth and death. And the Supreme Brahman who plays in Nanda's courtyard is Sri Krishna Himself. That is why the poet bows not to the Vedas, nor to the law-books, nor to the epic, but to the Lord of Vraja in whose courtyard the Absolute Truth plays: the Highest Truth is not the impersonal Brahman but the son of Nanda.

The Lord, filled with prema, longed to hear more, and Raghupati recited a second verse:

“When the Lord said, ‘Speak on,’ Upadhyaya continued, and Raghupati Upadhyaya bowed down before Him.

‘To whom can I tell it, and who would believe it now, that in the groves of the daughter of the Sun, the Yamuna, Brahman is the lover of the young cowherd girls?’ (Padyavali, 98).” (CC, Madhya 19.97–98)

The daughter of the Sun is Kalindi, the Yamuna. The word “lover” (vita; in the commentaries of Bhaktivinoda and Bhaktisiddhanta, lampata) belongs to the language of rasa-shastra, where it names the hero-lover. What is meant is not worldly passion but the transcendental prema of the gopis, the highest of rasas — and that is why the poet exclaims: who would believe that the Supreme Brahman, Whom men seek in the Vedas, has given Himself to the young cowherd girls of Vraja?5

The Lord asked him to go on, and Raghupati recited verses on Krishna's pastimes. Then Upadhyaya saw what he had not expected:

“The Lord said, ‘Go on,’ and he recited verses on Krishna's pastimes. In the ecstasy of love the Lord's body and mind were thrown into turmoil. Seeing such love, Upadhyaya was amazed. ‘He is not a human being,’ he concluded. ‘He is Krishna.’” (CC, Madhya 19.99–100)

Such love, Raghupati became firmly convinced, is never found in a human being. By its signs he recognised in Mahaprabhu Vrajendra-nandana Himself, the son of the king of Vraja — the very One of Whom he had just been reciting his verses.

A Conversation about the Highest

Then the Lord, like a disciple before a teacher, began to question Raghupati, and between them there arose an ishtagoshthi — an intimate talk about the degrees of excellence within the highest:

“The Lord said: ‘Upadhyaya, whom do you consider the best?’ ‘Shyamam eva param rupam — the dark form is the supreme form,’ said Upadhyaya. ‘Which abode of that dark form do you consider the best?’ ‘Puri madhu-puri vara — Madhupuri is the best of cities,’ said Upadhyaya. ‘Of childhood, boyhood and youth, which do you consider the best?’ ‘Vayah kaishorakam dhyeyam — youth is the age to meditate on,’ said Upadhyaya. ‘Among all the rasas, which do you consider the best?’ ‘Adya eva paro rasah — the original rasa is the highest,’ said Upadhyaya. The Lord said: ‘You have taught Me an excellent truth.’ Saying this, He recited the verse in a voice choked with emotion:

‘The dark form is the supreme form; Madhupuri is the best of cities; youth (kaishora) is the age to meditate on; and the original rasa, shringara, is the highest rasa’ (Padyavali, 82).” (CC, Madhya 19.101–106)6

The four questions lead ever higher. Of the countless forms of God — Krishna, Narayana, Rama, Nrisimha — the best is the form of Shyama; of His abodes the best is Madhupuri, Mathura; of the ages — childhood (balya), boyhood (pauganda) and youth (kaishora) — the best is kaishora; of the rasas, the original (adya). In these answers lies the highest object of worship. In the subheading of Srila Bhaktisiddhanta's edition this original rasa is called transcendental shringara, the highest of the rasas: it is the sweet love of the gopis for Krishna, madhurya-rasa, and that love is parakiya, not “conjugal.”7

The Lord's words “you have taught Me” are the play of One Who has taken the form of His own devotee: He asks about Himself to taste the sweetness of what He hears and to teach the world through His devotee's lips — just as He once questioned Ramananda Raya — and not at all because there was something He did not know. Srila Bhaktivinoda Thakura, summing up the chapter, says briefly: when Raghupati came, he and Mahaprabhu had many talks about rasa.

In the Lord's Embrace

“In His rapture the Lord embraced him, and Upadhyaya, intoxicated with love, began to dance. Seeing this, Vallabha Bhatta was amazed.” (CC, Madhya 19.107–108)8

So the learned pandita from Mithila, who had come with respectful prayers, broke into dance in the Lord's embrace, intoxicated with love.

His Verses in the “Padyavali”

Raghupati was the author of many verses steeped in bhakti-rasa, and Srila Rupa Gosvami, who had heard him himself in Adail, later included several of them in his anthology, the “Padyavali.” Srila Bhaktivinoda Thakura too notes that the “Padyavali” contains his verses. In the editions of the “Charitamrita” the verse “Shrutim apare…” is cited as “Padyavali” 126, “Kam prati…” as 98, and “Shyamam eva…” as 82.9

In the Bengali edition of the “Padyavali” of 1911 his name stands under other verses as well. One is a prayer: “Here our Lord called the calves, here He played the flute” — so, with tears, may my days pass on the bank of the Yamuna (no. 88). Another says that the shruti are like empty straw: the Supreme Brahman was long ago stolen away by the eyes of the cowherd girls (no. 98). A third, that the fruit of others' austerities has fallen to the young cowherd girls (no. 302).

The biographies also cite Raghupati's verses heard in Adail among the arguments about when the “Padyavali” was compiled: since Rupa included in it verses he had heard in Adail in the Lord's presence, the anthology took shape after that meeting.

Narahari Chakravarti, in the “Namamrita-samudra,” where his prayers call upon the Lord's associates, turns to him as well, asking for the true siddhanta:

“Sri Chandrashekhara, Raghupati Upadhyaya! Grant that the true siddhanta be revealed in my heart.” (“Namamrita-samudra” 48)

Significance

We know little of Raghupati Upadhyaya, but that little is a summit. In Vallabha's house, in the presence of Rupa Gosvami, the Lord by His questions drew from His devotee's lips the whole essence of the object of worship: Shyama, Mathura, kaishora and the original rasa of the gopis. And the poet himself, seeing the Lord's prema, understood to Whom he was reciting his verses.

His verse “Kam prati…” lives on in our line as well. On 17 March 1973 in Mayapur, at the opening of a temple, Srila B. S. Govinda Dev-Goswami Maharaj, at the request of his guru, Srila B. R. Sridhar Maharaj, began his talk with this verse and applied it to Srila A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada: who would believe that “Abhay Babu,” a householder burdened with family and business, had become an acharya for the whole world? So Raghupati's words about Krishna's inconceivable grace came to speak of a wonder worked by His will.

Notes

  1. One of the biographies, describing the ancient kingdom of Tirhut, names Sitamarhi instead of Saran: Darbhanga, Sitamarhi, Muzaffarpur and Champaran.
  2. The verse of the “Chaitanya-bhagavata” itself speaks only of Nityananda's meeting with Madhavendra: “In the course of His travels the Lord [Nityananda], by the will of providence, met Sri Madhavendra Puri” (CB, Adi 9.154); Srila Bhaktisiddhanta gives the list of Madhavendra's disciples in his commentary on this verse. The “Charitamrita,” in its account of Raghupati (Madhya 19), is silent about his discipleship.
  3. One of the biographies places the meeting “in Prayaga-dhama, in the house of Vallabhacharya.” According to the “Charitamrita” (Madhya 19.79–92), Vallabha's house stood in Adail, on the other bank of the Yamuna, opposite Prayaga.
  4. In the “Charitamrita” the order of events is different: Rupa came to the Lord before Vallabha invited Him to Adail, and Raghupati came there when Rupa was already present (Madhya 19.79–92). Kaviraja does not say that Raghupati received the Lord in Prayaga every day.
  5. In one of the biographies the word vita in the translation of this verse is rendered by an expression with a worldly colouring (“lusting”); for a Vaishnava such a reading is inadmissible. In the “Charitamrita” it is “the lover of the young cowherd girls.”
  6. The sources differ on who composed the verse “Shyamam eva…”. According to the “Charitamrita” (Madhya 19.105), it is the verse in which the Lord joined together all of Raghupati's answers. The Bengali edition of the “Padyavali” of 1911 puts his name under it (there it is no. 83), and one of the biographies also takes it as his composition; but in the subheading to Madhya 19.106 in Srila Bhaktisiddhanta's edition it is “a verse of Madhavendra Puri (‘Padyavali,’ 82).” We do not undertake to decide the question.
  7. One of the biographies renders the “original rasa” in English by a word that suggests worldly sensuality; this is wrong: the shringara of the gopis is transcendental prema. An earlier Russian translation of the “Charitamrita” had “the rasa of conjugal love” here, but the love of the gopis is parakiya, not conjugal.
  8. The biographies add that all of Vallabha's household were amazed at Raghupati's good fortune as well. In the “Charitamrita” (Madhya 19.108) it is Vallabha himself who is amazed — “at all that had happened”; the verse says nothing of his household.
  9. In the Bengali edition of the “Padyavali” of 1911 (and in one of the biographies) the numbers are one higher: “Shrutim apare” is 127, “Kam prati” 99, “Shyamam eva” 83; this is a difference of editions, not an error.
